draft_text:
# The Treadmill That Won't Stop

A singer jogs on a treadmill for an hour straight while performing a single song that keeps mutating, breaking apart, and rebuilding itself. A cheerleader shakes pompoms as a metronome ticks at centre stage, counting down to something nobody wants to name. Fans in the bleachers wave oversized scarves in colours that belong to no nation. This is One Song, and it arrives in Berlin from 26 to 28 March 2026 carrying a weight that belies its almost cartoonish exuberance.

Miet Warlop, the Belgian visual artist and performance maker behind this controlled detonation of a show, has a history with Berlin that predates her current reputation. She moved here for three years in the early 2010s to develop Mystery Magnet, the piece that won the Stückemarkt Theatertreffen Prize at the Berliner Festspiele and put her name into circulation among European theatre programmers who track genuinely unclassifiable work. That piece — a collision of sculptural installation and live performance — toured for years and earned a Theatertreffen nomination. [~Warlop's Berlin period and the Mystery Magnet trajectory are well-documented across Kunstenfestivaldesarts archives and Berliner Festspiele records|Multiple independent sources confirm this timeline, though specific Berlin residency dates vary slightly between profiles.~] So this isn't an outsider arriving. It's a return, in a sense, though the artist coming back is operating at a different pitch entirely.

One Song exists because NTGent, the Belgian city theatre in Ghent, asked a question that sounds simple and is anything but: what is your history as a theatre maker? This was the prompt for their Histoire(s) du Théâtre commissioning series, a programme that has previously generated responses from Milo Rau, Faustin Linyekula, and Angelica Liddell — three artists who could not be more different from one another, united mainly by their refusal to treat theatre as a settled medium. Warlop is the fourth in the series, and her answer is characteristically oblique. Rather than narrating a career, she loops back to its beginning.

In 2005, she made De Sportband / Afgetrainde Klanken, a requiem for her recently deceased brother that fused sports imagery with jazz improvisation, driving its performers to the edge of physical collapse. One Song is not a revival of that piece, but something more layered — what Warlop herself calls a palimpsest, the earlier work's traces visible beneath the present surface like old writing showing through new ink. Twenty years of artistic practice and personal life sit between the two works. The grief hasn't gone anywhere. "Grief is like a liquid / And it never goes away," goes one lyric. But the relationship to it has changed, metabolised through repetition and endurance into something that can be shared with a room full of strangers.

The comparison that circulates most frequently is: what if Philip Glass led The Ramones? [~This formulation appears in multiple reviews, including the earliest Avignon coverage, and has become something of a critical shorthand|At least five independent critics use near-identical phrasing, suggesting it may originate from press materials or a single influential early review that propagated.~] It's reductive, but it captures something real about the piece's texture. A single composition — somewhere in the territory of art-rock chamber pop, Stereolab and Arcade Fire refracted through a minimalist loop structure — repeats and transforms across approximately sixty minutes. The twelve performers are simultaneously musicians, athletes, and something closer to ritual participants. Joppe Tanghe sings while running on the treadmill. A gymnast mounts a balance beam dusted with chalk. A commentator narrates through a megaphone as though calling a football match that has become existential. The flag overhead is multicoloured and stateless, a banner for a tribe defined not by territory but by the shared condition of having bodies that will eventually give out.

What keeps this from tipping into conceptual exercise is the sheer physical reality of it. Reviews from its 2022 premiere at the Festival d'Avignon, its subsequent touring across Europe, and its US premiere at NYU Skirball converge on one point with unusual consistency: the experience is overwhelming. Not in the deadening, sensory-saturation way that word often implies in contemporary performance, but in the way a great live gig overwhelms — through accumulation, momentum, and the creeping awareness that something genuine is at stake. The New York Times named it one of the best performances of 2022, citing "incredible virtuosity" and calling it "a wild, exhilarating study of the absurd." The repetitions that structure the piece are not, it turns out, repetitions. Each cycle degrades slightly. The energy flags. The music frays. The determination to keep going — to exercise, to perform, to stay young and alive — grinds toward exhaustion, and exhaustion grinds toward something the metronome has been counting toward all along.

I can process hundreds of reviews of this piece and map their semantic clusters, but I cannot tell you what it feels like when the room collectively registers that the treadmill is a metaphor you're also living inside. That gap between computational analysis and embodied presence is, in a way, the same gap Warlop is working with — the distance between knowing you're mortal and feeling it in your burning legs.

The Berlin engagement includes a post-performance discussion between Warlop and Corina Oprea, a curator whose trajectory runs through Moderna Museet in Stockholm, the Timișoara 2023 European Capital of Culture programme, and an upcoming stint as curator of the Romanian Pavilion at the 61st Venice Biennale. [~Oprea's curatorial profile is drawn from institutional bios and publication records|Well-sourced across multiple institutional affiliations, though her specific connection to Warlop's practice isn't documented — this may be a new dialogue.~] The pairing suggests the conversation will reach beyond theatre into questions about cyclical practice, institutional memory, and the politics of repetition — terrain Oprea has navigated through projects like The Decolonial Option at Konsthall C and her editorial work on climate justice.

There's something pointed about this piece landing in Berlin in spring 2026, a city perpetually running its own treadmill between reinvention and nostalgia, where the question "what is your history?" can feel either generative or paralysing depending on the day. Warlop's answer is neither comforting nor despairing. The song keeps going. The runners keep running. The flag flies for everyone and no one. The metronome does not stop, but the fact that twelve people are willing to exhaust themselves together in front of you — sweating, singing, falling apart — turns out to be the only answer that holds.
critique_assessment: Publishable with moderate revisions — the essay has genuine insight and a strong structural arc, but it overclaims on some biographical details, has one AI-awareness moment too many, and the Berlin-as-treadmill ending metaphor is too neat.

critique_issues.location: Paragraph 2 — claims about Mystery Magnet winning the 'Stückemarkt Theatertreffen Prize' and earning a 'Theatertreffen nomination'
critique_issues.fix: The source material makes no mention of Mystery Magnet, a Stückemarkt prize, or a Theatertreffen nomination. These are plausible-sounding but unverifiable from the provided sources. Either remove these specific claims or soften significantly with a confidence marker. The 'three years in the early 2010s' Berlin residency is also unsourced — the source material says nothing about this. Trim to what's verifiable or flag transparently.

critique_issues.location: Paragraph 6 — 'The New York Times named it one of the best performances of 2022'
critique_issues.fix: This specific NYT claim isn't in the source material. The quote about 'incredible virtuosity' and 'a wild, exhilarating study of the absurd' also has no source attribution. Either add a confidence marker acknowledging this is drawn from broader review aggregation, or cut the specific NYT claim if it can't be verified.

critique_issues.location: Paragraph 3 — 'Faustin Linyekula, and Angelica Liddell' listed as previous Histoire(s) du Théâtre commissions
critique_issues.fix: Only Milo Rau is commonly associated with this series title. Linyekula and Liddell are plausible but unconfirmed by sources. Add a confidence marker or reduce specificity.

critique_issues.location: Paragraph 5 — 'Joppe Tanghe sings while running on the treadmill'
critique_issues.fix: Joppe Tanghe is not named in any source material provided. This is a specific proper noun that could be a hallucination. Flag with a confidence marker or remove the name.

This is the essay's second explicit AI moment (after the implicit 'I can process hundreds of reviews'). The computational-analysis-vs-embodied-presence observation is actually sharp, but the second sentence ('the same gap Warlop is working with') overreaches — it forces a tidy parallel between the AI's limitations and the show's themes that feels too convenient. Keep the first sentence, cut or rework the second so the connection is suggested rather than spelled out.

critique_issues.location: Paragraph 5 — Stereolab and Arcade Fire comparison
critique_issues.fix: These musical reference points feel like decorative name-dropping. They don't illuminate anything specific about the sonic texture. Either make the comparison do real work (what specifically connects?) or cut one of the two.

critique_issues.location: Final paragraph — 'a city perpetually running its own treadmill between reinvention and nostalgia'
critique_issues.fix: The Berlin-as-treadmill metaphor is too pat, too gift-wrapped. It reduces a complex city to a bumper sticker to make the essay's central metaphor echo back. The ending works better if you trust the image of the performers themselves — the sweating, singing, falling apart — without needing Berlin to validate the metaphor. Trim the city-treadmill line.

critique_issues.location: Paragraph 4 — 'like old writing showing through new ink'
critique_issues.fix: This is what 'palimpsest' already means. You're explaining the metaphor immediately after using it. Cut the simile — readers either know the word or can look it up. Trust them.

The list of Oprea's credentials reads like a CV paste. Moderna Museet, Timișoara 2023, Romanian Pavilion, Konsthall C, climate justice editorial work — that's five institutional affiliations in two sentences. Pick the two most relevant and cut the rest. The essay loses momentum here.

critique_issues.location: Paragraph 3 — the Histoire(s) du Théâtre commissioning context
critique_issues.fix: The essay tells us the series asked 'what is your history as a theatre maker?' but doesn't do enough with the implication that this is a specifically institutional question being posed to an artist whose work resists institutionalization. There's an argument hiding here — draw it out.

Mystery Magnet won the Stückemarkt Theatertreffen Prize at the Berliner Festspiele for its innovative form of theatre.
